title: pandas: load, inspect, select, filter, group
story:
An array has positions. Data work needs names, because the thing in row 4,891 is a customer, not a position, and the moment two tables have to be compared the position stops meaning anything at all.

That is the addition the table makes: labels on the axes, and operations that line up on the labels rather than on where things happen to sit. McKinney presented it at the Python in Science Conference in 2010, having started building it at AQR Capital Management in 2008 and open sourced it in 2009; the paper is explicit that automatic data alignment was a central design concern and that the comparison in view was the R language. Everything good about the tool and the one thing that will bite you both come from that decision.

The aggregation half has an older and wider pedigree than the library. Wickham named and analysed the split-apply-combine strategy in the Journal of Statistical Software in 2011 — break a large problem into manageable pieces, operate on each independently, reassemble the results — and explicitly framed it as a strategy that applies regardless of how the data is stored. That is why the same verb appears in the query language, in the R packages, and in the distributed engines: grouping is not a feature of any one of them.

Now the bite. Alignment is silent in both directions. It will line up two objects you meant to line up, which is the feature and saves you the bookkeeping. It will equally line up two objects you did not, and the result has the right shape and the wrong contents. Add two columns of the same length whose indexes are in different orders and you do not get an error; you get element-wise addition by label, which is arithmetic between rows that have nothing to do with one another. The shape is right, the type is right, the numbers are wrong, and the only thing that would have told you is an index you never looked at.

One trap that used to belong here has been closed, and it is worth knowing it is gone rather than repeating it. For years the ambiguity over whether an indexing operation returned a view or a copy produced a famous warning and a habit of defensive copying. Copy-on-write became the default and only mode in version 3.0, released in January 2026: everything returned from an indexing operation now behaves as an independent copy, the warning was removed because the ambiguity no longer exists, and chained assignment fails loudly instead of quietly doing nothing. If you learned this tool before then, unlearn the workaround.

problem.name: Labelled axes
problem.shape: Two collections of values have to be combined, and what makes a pair of values correspond is an identity rather than a position.
tell: arithmetic between two columns that came from different operations
one of the inputs is the result of a sort, a filter or a grouped aggregation
the result has exactly the right shape and numbers that cannot be right
the index has never been inspected, only carried
problem.move: Decide, at every operation between two labelled objects, whether you mean positional or aligned arithmetic. For positional, drop to the underlying values. For aligned, assert that the indexes match before operating, so that a mismatch stops the program. Reset the index deliberately after anything that rearranged it, rather than as a reflex to make a warning go away.
problem.invariant: Any operation between two labelled objects is a join on their labels. Correspondence is by identity, never by position, and that holds whether or not the code was written with a join in mind.
problem.breaks: Alignment cannot tell a meaningful label from an accidental one. A default integer index that survives a sort is still a label, so the operation dutifully joins on row numbers that no longer mean anything — the mechanism works perfectly on labels that stopped carrying identity several steps earlier.

cost.time: an index assertion before combining, which is one comparison against a class of bug that produces no symptom at all
cost.space: the index itself, which is an extra column's worth of memory and the price of the entire abstraction
cost.beats: manual positional bookkeeping, which is what the labels replaced and which fails in the opposite direction — silently misaligned the moment either side is reordered

worked.problem: You added two columns of the same length and got the wrong answer. Nothing raised, and the result has exactly the shape you expected.
worked.reasoning:
Because they were added by label, not by position, and their labels were not in the same order.

Labelled axes are the point of the structure. An operation between two objects does not assume that the thing in position three of one corresponds to the thing in position three of the other — it matches them on their index. That is what makes joining, reindexing and arithmetic across differently ordered tables work without manual bookkeeping, and it is the behaviour the library was designed around.

The same rule applies when you did not mean it to. If one column came back from a sort, a filter that preserved original labels, a group operation, or a read that assigned its own index, then its labels are in a different order from the other's. Adding them pairs label with label. Every value is arithmetic between two rows that have no relationship, the result has the right length and the right type, and nothing is exceptional enough to report.

The tell is that the answer is wrong but plausible, and the shape is perfect. If the indexes were merely different rather than reordered — disjoint labels, say — you would get missing values appearing where no label matched, which at least looks wrong. Reordered labels give you a full column of confident nonsense.

The fixes are all about making the intent explicit. Reset the index after any operation that may have preserved or rearranged it, and do it deliberately rather than as a reflex. If you genuinely want positional arithmetic, take the underlying values and operate on those, which drops the labels and therefore the alignment. If you want aligned arithmetic, assert first that the two indexes are equal, so that a mismatch stops the program rather than producing a number.

And the general point: automatic alignment is not a convenience layered on top of the data, it is the semantics. Any operation between two labelled objects is a join whether or not you were thinking of it as one.
worked.code:
THE FEATURE AND THE BUG ARE THE SAME LINE

  arrays have POSITIONS
  tables have LABELS, and operations align on them

  s1 = [1, 2, 3]   index [0, 1, 2]
  s2 = [1, 2, 3]   index [2, 1, 0]      <- reversed

  s1 + s2   ==   [4, 4, 4]

     not [2, 4, 6].
     right length. right dtype. wrong numbers.
     nothing raised.

  because it paired LABEL 0 with LABEL 0:
     s1[0]=1  +  s2[0]=3  ->  4
     s1[1]=2  +  s2[1]=2  ->  4
     s1[2]=3  +  s2[2]=1  ->  4

WHERE A REORDERED INDEX COMES FROM

  a sort
  a filter that preserved original labels
  a grouped result
  a read that assigned its own index

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A DISJOINT INDEX

  disjoint labels -> missing values appear
                     (at least it LOOKS wrong)
  reordered       -> a full column of confident
                     nonsense

THE THREE FIXES, BY INTENT

  positional?   take the underlying values.
                no labels -> no alignment.
  aligned?      assert the indexes are equal
                FIRST, so a mismatch stops the
                program instead of returning a
                number.
  unsure?       reset the index deliberately
                after anything that rearranged it.

CLOSED, AS OF VERSION 3.0 (JANUARY 2026)

  copy-on-write is the only mode now.
  the view-or-copy ambiguity is gone,
  the old warning was REMOVED,
  chained assignment now RAISES.

  if you learned the defensive-copy habit
  before then: unlearn it.

problem.practice: Make two columns holding the same three values, one with its index reversed, and add them. Then reproduce the same failure the way it actually occurs: sort one table, take a column from it, and combine it with a column from the unsorted original. Finally, write the assertion that would have caught it, and put that assertion in a function you already have.

beats.broke: An array has positions and no names, so every comparison between two tables becomes manual bookkeeping about which row number currently means which entity.
beats.fix: Put labels on the axes and align operations on the labels rather than on position — the design concern named in the 2010 paper — and express aggregation as split-apply-combine, the strategy Wickham analysed in 2011, which belongs to no single library.
beats.cost: Alignment is silent in both directions. It joins the objects you meant to join, and equally the ones you did not, returning a result of the right shape and the wrong contents — and a default index that survived a sort is still a label the operation will faithfully use.

interview.q: You added two columns of the same length and got the wrong answer. Nothing raised, and the result has exactly the shape you expected.
interview.trap: Hunting for a bug in the arithmetic, or reaching for a reset of the index until the numbers look right. The arithmetic is correct; it was performed between the pairs the labels specified, and changing the index until the output looks plausible is how the wrong answer gets shipped.
interview.answer:
Because the addition aligned on labels rather than on positions, and the two sets of labels were in different orders.

Labelled axes are the whole point of the structure. An operation between two objects does not assume that position three of one corresponds to position three of the other; it matches on the index. That is what lets you combine differently ordered tables without manual bookkeeping, and the library was designed around it.

The rule does not switch off when you forget about it. If one of the columns came out of a sort, a filter that kept the original labels, a grouped result, or a read that assigned its own index, its labels are in a different order — and the addition then pairs label with label. Every element is arithmetic between two unrelated rows. The length is right, the type is right, and nothing is exceptional enough to raise.

What makes it nastier than the alternative failure is that it looks fine. Disjoint labels would produce missing values where nothing matched, which at least reads as wrong. Reordered labels give a complete column of plausible numbers.

I would fix it by making the intent explicit. For positional arithmetic, operate on the underlying values, which have no labels and therefore no alignment. For aligned arithmetic, assert that the two indexes are equal before the operation, so a mismatch stops the program instead of returning an answer. And reset the index deliberately after any step that might have rearranged it.

The underlying point is that alignment is the semantics, not a convenience. Any operation between two labelled objects is a join, whether or not you were thinking of it as one.

takeaway: Labels on the axes are what make a row mean an entity rather than a position — and because every operation between two labelled objects is a join on those labels, the feature that saves the bookkeeping will also align two things you never meant to align and hand back the right shape with the wrong numbers.
